# Salt making (sea salt, brine boiling, rock salt) (`salt_production`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Core idea: Sea water holds about 3.5 % salt. Let it evaporate in a chain of shallow clay pans: gypsum settles first, common salt crystallises once the brine is about ten times concentrated, and the bitter mother liquor that remains must be drained off. Stronger inland brines from springs or wells are boiled in wide pans; rock salt is mined or dissolved underground. Salt preserves meat, fish and vegetables (dry salting or a brine strong enough to float an egg), and is the raw material for soda, hydrochloric acid and chlorine.
- Pitfalls:
  - Evaporating to dryness: the magnesium salts make the product bitter, damp and purgative.
  - Boiling brine in lead pans, which contaminates the salt.
  - Underestimating fuel; boiling weak brine takes many times the salt's weight in wood. Concentrate it first by sun and wind.
  - Salt does not prevent goitre unless it carries iodine; inland rock salt usually has none.
- History: europe: c. 6000 BC – brine boiling in pottery at Poiana Slatinei (Romania); from c. 1500 BC salt mining at Hallstatt; 16th c. graduation towers concentrate weak brine; china: c. 2000 BC – salt works at Zhongba; c. 250 BC Li Bing's brine wells in Sichuan; 11th c. percussion-drilled wells over 100 m deep; 1835 a well passes 1000 m; mesopotamia: 3rd millennium BC – salt gathered from marshes and traded; egypt: from Old Kingdom – salt and natron from desert lakes; salted fish; africa: medieval – caravans carried Taghaza salt to West African markets; Taoudenni succeeded Taghaza in the late 16th c.; americas: c. 1000 BC onwards – Maya coastal salt works; Andean brine pans at Maras; india: ancient – sea salt pans in Gujarat and salt from the Punjab Salt Range
- Read:
  - Robert P. Multhauf, Neptune's Gift: A History of Common Salt (1978)
  - Mark Kurlansky, Salt: A World History (2002)
